title: Tosca
facts: Tosca premiered at the Teatro Costanzi in Rome on 14 January 1900, a day late, because of fears of unrest.
Police had warnings of an anarchist bomb at the premiere. The conductor, Mugnone, was told to strike up the royal march in an emergency.
The critics were lukewarm, but the public loved it: the premiere was followed by twenty performances, all to packed houses.
Puccini begged his publisher in 1889 to get Sardou’s permission: “I see in this Tosca the opera I need, with no overblown proportions, no elaborate spectacle.”
Puccini, letter to Giulio Ricordi, 7 May 1889 (via Wikipedia)
The young Enrico Caruso hoped to create Cavaradossi but was passed over for the more experienced Emilio De Marchi.
There is no prelude: the opening chords are Scarpia’s motif, and Angelotti bursts straight in.
As the Te Deum procession fills the church, Scarpia joins the prayer: “Tosca, you make me forget even God!”
Maria Jeritza, said to be Puccini’s favorite Tosca, once fell while escaping Scarpia and sang “Vissi d’arte” lying on the floor. It was such a success that she kept doing it.
For the Roman dawn, Puccini went to Castel Sant’Angelo to hear the matins bells, and had bells cast by four different foundries.
Librettist Illica grumbled after the premiere that all the fuss and money spent on the bells “passes completely unnoticed”.
Luigi Illica, letter to Ricordi (via Wikipedia)
The shepherd boy’s song is in Roman dialect. Puccini asked for a “good romanesco poet”, and folklorist Giggi Zanazzo wrote the verse.
Ricordi noticed that part of “O dolci mani” was borrowed from music Puccini had cut from his early opera Edgar, and demanded changes. There wasn’t time.
In the 1950s musicologist Joseph Kerman called Tosca a “shabby little shocker”. Conductor Thomas Beecham replied that anything Kerman says about Puccini “can safely be ignored”.
The Met premiere was on 4 February 1901, only a year after the world premiere.
Luciano Pavarotti’s last stage performance was as Cavaradossi at the Met, on 13 March 2004.
Sardou’s play La Tosca, written for Sarah Bernhardt, had more than 3,000 performances in France alone.
By cutting several numbers, Puccini left “three strong characters trapped in an airless, violent, tightly wound melodrama”, as his biographer put it.
Mary Jane Phillips-Matz, Puccini biography (via Wikipedia)
